name: A stricter AppArmor profile + fix a missing profile
objective: CKS › System Hardening (15%). Drill EVERY AppArmor corner harder than the exam: write + load a profile on a node with apparmor_parser, understand profile-name vs filename, reference it from a pod via the typed appArmorProfile field (Localhost / RuntimeDefault / Unconfined), prove a denied write is blocked, contrast confined vs unconfined, load a second stricter profile, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix for a pod stuck on a missing profile. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Load a second, stricter profile (deny network)
questions.teach:
AppArmor rules go beyond files: `deny network,` blocks all socket use. Write a second profile `k8s-deny-net` and load it alongside the first — a node can hold many loaded profiles, each tracked by its own profile name.

**Gotcha:** reloading one profile with `apparmor_parser -r` does not touch others; use `-R` to **remove** a profile. Loading a new file never un-loads `k8s-deny-write`.
questions.prompt:
On `$W1`, write `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-net` (profile name `k8s-deny-net`) that **denies all network access** (`deny network,`), and load it with `apparmor_parser`. Leave `k8s-deny-write` loaded.

Target: file `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-net` on `$W1` has `profile k8s-deny-net` and a `deny network,` rule.
questions.hint: Same heredoc-into-tee approach as Step 1. Body: `profile k8s-deny-net flags=(attach_disconnected) { #include <abstractions/base>` + `network,` + `deny network,` + `}`. Load with `apparmor_parser -r -W`.

verification.description: /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-net on $W1 has profile name k8s-deny-net + deny network rule

questions.eli5:
Last time your rule-book locked a *drawer* (writing files). This time you write a second, different rule-book that pulls the *phone line* out of the wall: `deny network,` means the confined program can't open any sockets — no outbound connections, no listening, no talking to the network at all.

Think of a node as a building that can hold a whole **shelf of rule-books**. Adding a new one, `k8s-deny-net`, doesn't throw the old `k8s-deny-write` off the shelf — both sit there side by side, each known by its own name. You write the file into `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-net` and load it with `apparmor_parser -r -W`, exactly like before.

The important mental shift: **loading a profile only affects that one profile.** `-r` reloads/replaces *the file you point it at*. It never touches the others. So after this step the node has two independent locks available, and the first one is still perfectly intact.

**Watch out for:**

- `-r` **reloads one** profile; it does **not** remove or disturb any other loaded profile. To actually *unload* a profile you use `-R` (capital R).
- Loading `k8s-deny-net` leaves `k8s-deny-write` loaded — don't assume a new file replaces the old one.
- Profile name vs filename still matters: the name after `profile` (`k8s-deny-net`) is what pods ask for; keep it matching the filename.
- `deny network,` blocks *all* networking — a program that needs DNS or any socket will break under it. That's the point, but know the blast radius.
- Every rule still needs its trailing comma, and use a quoted heredoc so `$` isn't mangled.
- Confirm with `aa-status` that **both** profiles now show up.
questions.deepDive:
## A second, stricter profile (deny network) + managing multiple profiles — full rundown

### Mental model
AppArmor rules aren't limited to files. A profile can also constrain **network** access, **capabilities**, **mount**, **ptrace**, signals, and more. Here you add `deny network,` — a blanket ban on socket creation. A node holds a **set** of loaded profiles, each independent and tracked by its own profile name; loading one never disturbs another.

### The network-deny profile
```text
#include <tunables/global>

profile k8s-deny-net flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  #include <abstractions/base>

  file,
  network,                 # the capability area being governed...
  deny network,            # ...and the explicit blanket deny
}
```
- `network,` by itself would *allow* networking. The `deny network,` line is what actually blocks it; `deny` always overrides allow.
- You can scope network rules more finely: `deny network inet,` (IPv4), `network inet tcp,` (allow only TCP/IPv4), `network inet6 udp,`, etc.

### Network rule grammar (useful subset)
| Rule | Effect |
|---|---|
| `network,` | allow all socket families/types |
| `deny network,` | deny all networking |
| `network inet tcp,` | allow IPv4 TCP only |
| `network inet udp,` | allow IPv4 UDP only |
| `deny network inet6,` | deny all IPv6 |
| `network unix,` | allow Unix-domain sockets |

### apparmor_parser flags — the ones that matter
| Flag | Action |
|---|---|
| `-a` | **add** a profile (fails if already loaded) |
| `-r` | **replace/reload** — load, or re-load if already present (idempotent; use this) |
| `-R` | **remove** a profile from the kernel |
| `-W` | **wait** until the operation completes before returning |
| `-C` / `aa-complain` | load in **complain** mode (log, don't block) |

> Key exam point: **`-r` touches only the profile in the file you pass.** It never unloads others. To remove `k8s-deny-write` you'd run `apparmor_parser -R /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-write` — nothing else.

### Loading alongside the first profile (kind)
```bash
docker exec -i "$W1" tee /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-net >/dev/null <<'EOF'
#include <tunables/global>
profile k8s-deny-net flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  #include <abstractions/base>
  file,
  network,
  deny network,
}
EOF
docker exec "$W1" apparmor_parser -r -W /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-net

# both profiles now loaded, independently
docker exec "$W1" aa-status | grep -E 'k8s-deny-(write|net)'
```

### Verifying multiple profiles are loaded
```bash
docker exec "$W1" aa-status
# ... profiles are in enforce mode.
#   k8s-deny-net
#   k8s-deny-write
docker exec "$W1" cat /sys/kernel/security/apparmor/profiles | grep k8s-
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`-r` ≠ remove.** Reloading one profile leaves all others loaded. Removal is `-R` (capital).
- **`deny network,` is total** — a confined app loses DNS, service calls, everything. Expect it to break unless the app is purely local. Scope with `network inet tcp,` style rules when you need partial access.
- You must include a `network,` grant area (and then the `deny`) — `deny` works on rule classes you've acknowledged; omit `network,` and behaviour can differ by parser version.
- Profile name (`k8s-deny-net`) vs filename: pods reference the **name**; keep them equal.
- Trailing commas on every rule; quoted heredoc (`<<'EOF'`) so the shell leaves the body alone.
- `-W` avoids a race where a referencing pod starts before the profile is fully applied.
- Loading a new file does **not** replace a previously loaded profile with a different name — don't assume "newest wins."

### Quick reference
```bash
# add a second profile without disturbing the first
docker exec "$W1" apparmor_parser -r -W /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-net
docker exec "$W1" aa-status | grep k8s-                 # both listed
# to unload one later:
docker exec "$W1" apparmor_parser -R /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-net
```

questions.title: Bind the stricter profile to a pod
questions.teach:
Each loaded profile is referenced by name. Point a pod at `k8s-deny-net` the same way as `k8s-deny-write`: `type: Localhost`, `localhostProfile: k8s-deny-net`, pinned to the node where it is loaded.

**Gotcha:** `localhostProfile` is a bare profile name — not `localhost/k8s-deny-net` and not a file path. The `localhost/` prefix belongs only to the old beta annotation.
questions.prompt:
In `cks-apparmor`, create pod `netlocked` on node `$W1`, image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`, container `hello`, referencing Localhost profile `k8s-deny-net`.

Target: pod `netlocked` on `$W1`, container `hello` has `appArmorProfile.type: Localhost`, `localhostProfile: k8s-deny-net`.
questions.hint: Identical shape to Step 2 but `localhostProfile: k8s-deny-net`. The value is the bare profile name (no `localhost/` prefix).
questions.solution:
cat <<YAML | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: netlocked
  namespace: cks-apparmor
spec:
  nodeName: $W1
  containers:
  - name: hello
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:
      appArmorProfile:
        type: Localhost
        localhostProfile: k8s-deny-net
YAML

verification.description: pod 'netlocked' on $W1, container hello → Localhost profile k8s-deny-net

questions.eli5:
You've got two rule-books on the shelf now. This step is pure muscle-memory: point a brand-new pod, `netlocked`, at the *second* one (`k8s-deny-net`) exactly the way you pointed `confined` at the first one.

Each rule-book on the shelf has its own name, and a pod asks for the one it wants by that name. So you give `netlocked` the same kind of badge — `type: Localhost`, `localhostProfile: k8s-deny-net` — and pin it to node `$W1` where that rule-book lives. Now that container runs with no network access at all.

The only thing that changes from the earlier Localhost step is the **name** you write in `localhostProfile`. Everything else is copy-paste.

**Watch out for:**

- `localhostProfile` is the **bare name**: `k8s-deny-net`. Not `localhost/k8s-deny-net`, not a file path like `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-net`. The `localhost/` prefix belongs only to the old beta annotation, never to this field.
- The profile must already be **loaded on the node the pod lands on** — that's why you pin to `$W1`. A missing profile means the pod won't start.
- Pointing at `k8s-deny-net` instead of `k8s-deny-write` is the whole difference; double-check you typed the right one.
- The field lives under the **container's** `securityContext` when you want just that container confined.

## Binding a specific loaded profile to a pod by name — full rundown

### Mental model
Every loaded AppArmor profile is addressed by its **profile name**. A pod selects *which* loaded profile to use through `localhostProfile`. Binding a second profile is mechanically identical to binding the first — you only change the name. This reinforces the core rule: **profile name is the handle; filename and path are irrelevant to the pod.**

### The manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: netlocked
  namespace: cks-apparmor
spec:
  nodeName: kindlab-worker            # node where k8s-deny-net is loaded
  containers:
  - name: hello
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:
      appArmorProfile:
        type: Localhost
        localhostProfile: k8s-deny-net   # bare name — the ONLY change vs k8s-deny-write
```

### The value format — three ways to write "the same" thing (and which is right)
| Context | Correct value |
|---|---|
| GA field `localhostProfile` | `k8s-deny-net` (bare name) |
| Beta annotation value | `localhost/k8s-deny-net` (with prefix) |
| Wrong everywhere | `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-net` (a file path) |

### Proving the network denial
```bash
# profile the container is confined by
kubectl -n cks-apparmor exec netlocked -- cat /proc/1/attr/current
# -> k8s-deny-net (enforce)

# any network attempt is blocked by the kernel
kubectl -n cks-apparmor exec netlocked -- sh -c 'wget -T2 -qO- http://example.com' 2>&1
# -> Permission denied / socket: Operation not permitted
```
Contrast with a pod bound to `k8s-deny-write`, where the network works but writing `/etc/secret-data/` fails — same mechanism, different rule set, selected purely by name.

### Verifying the binding
```bash
kubectl -n cks-apparmor get pod netlocked \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].securityContext.appArmorProfile}'; echo
# {"localhostProfile":"k8s-deny-net","type":"Localhost"}

kubectl -n cks-apparmor get pod netlocked -o wide     # confirm it's on $W1
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Bare name, no `localhost/` prefix, no path** in `localhostProfile`. The `localhost/` prefix is only for the deprecated beta annotation.
- **Wrong profile name silently confines to the wrong thing** or, if not loaded, stops the pod from starting. Confirm the exact spelling against `aa-status`.
- **Profile must be loaded on the landing node** — pin with `nodeName` (or label-select nodes that have it). A `Localhost` reference to an unloaded profile fails to start the pod.
- `type: Localhost` **requires** `localhostProfile`; the two always travel together.
- The only intended difference from the earlier Localhost pod is the profile **name** — a stray `k8s-deny-write` here binds the wrong rule set and fails grading.

### Quick reference
```yaml
securityContext:
  appArmorProfile:
    type: Localhost
    localhostProfile: k8s-deny-net    # bare name of a profile loaded on this node
```
```bash
kubectl -n cks-apparmor exec netlocked -- cat /proc/1/attr/current   # -> k8s-deny-net (enforce)
```

questions.title: Diagnose & fix: a pod stuck on a missing profile
questions.teach:
A pod requesting `type: Localhost` with a profile that is **not loaded on its node** will not start — the kubelet rejects it (on an AppArmor host the pod is `Blocked`/fails scheduling). `kubectl describe pod` shows the AppArmor error naming the missing profile.

**Gotcha:** fix it at the **node**, not the pod — write and load that exact profile name with `apparmor_parser`; don't just delete and rebuild the pod.
questions.prompt:
Pod `broken-aa` in `cks-apparmor` is pinned to `$W1` and references Localhost profile `k8s-audit-write`, but that profile was never written or loaded on `$W1`. Diagnose and fix so the referenced profile exists and is loaded. Create the profile file at `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-audit-write` (profile name `k8s-audit-write`) denying writes under `/etc/secret-data/`, and load it. Do not delete the pod.

Target: file `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-audit-write` on `$W1` has `profile k8s-audit-write` + a deny-write rule for `/etc/secret-data/`, AND `broken-aa` still references it.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n cks-apparmor describe pod broken-aa` shows the missing-profile error. Write `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-audit-write` (profile name `k8s-audit-write`, `deny /etc/secret-data/** w,`) via `docker exec -i "$W1" tee ...`, then `docker exec "$W1" apparmor_parser -r -W /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-audit-write`.

verification.description: k8s-audit-write profile written + loaded on $W1 AND broken-aa still references it

questions.eli5:
Here's a broken situation to untangle. Someone created a pod, `broken-aa`, that insists: *"confine me with the rule-book named `k8s-audit-write`."* Trouble is, nobody ever wrote or loaded that rule-book onto the node. The pod is asking for a book that isn't on the shelf — so it just won't start. The kubelet refuses: *"I can't find the AppArmor profile you asked for."*

Your job is to be the detective and the fixer. First, look at the pod's complaints with `kubectl describe pod broken-aa` — the Events will literally name the missing profile. Then here's the key insight: **the pod isn't wrong, the node is missing something.** So you fix it at the *node*, not the pod. You write the missing rule-book `k8s-audit-write` into `/etc/apparmor.d/`, give it the matching deny-write rule, and load it with `apparmor_parser`. The kubelet keeps retrying, and once the profile exists the pod finally starts — no need to touch the pod at all.

**Watch out for:**

- Fix the **node**, not the pod. Don't delete and recreate `broken-aa` — the task wants the profile to exist, and the existing pod to keep referencing it.
- The profile name inside the file must be **exactly** `k8s-audit-write` (matching what the pod asked for), or the pod still can't find it.
- Write the file to the node the pod is pinned to (`$W1`) — loading it elsewhere won't help.
- Use `describe pod` to read the real error; the Events section names the missing profile for you.
- Don't invent a different profile name or edit the pod to point somewhere else — supply what it already asks for.
- Same syntax rules as before: trailing commas, quoted heredoc, `apparmor_parser -r -W`.
questions.deepDive:
## Diagnose & fix: a pod stuck on a missing AppArmor profile — full rundown

### Mental model
A pod with `appArmorProfile.type: Localhost` names a profile that **must already be loaded on the node where it lands**. If that profile is absent, the kubelet cannot honour the request and **refuses to start the container** — the pod does not run. The resolution is to supply what the pod asks for **on the node**, not to change the pod. Profile resolution happens at pod admission/startup on the node, so you fix it node-side and let the kubelet retry.

### Step 1 — diagnose
```bash
kubectl -n cks-apparmor describe pod broken-aa | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
# Warning  Failed   kubelet  Error: failed to get container spec opts:
#   failed to generate apparmor spec opts: apparmor profile not found k8s-audit-write
```
Also check *where* it's pinned and *what* it asked for:
```bash
kubectl -n cks-apparmor get pod broken-aa -o wide
kubectl -n cks-apparmor get pod broken-aa \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].securityContext.appArmorProfile}'; echo
# {"localhostProfile":"k8s-audit-write","type":"Localhost"}
```
What the pod's state looks like depends on the node/runtime: it may sit `Pending`/`ContainerCreating` or report a `Blocked`/`CreateContainerError`-style failure — in all cases the Events name the missing profile.

### Step 2 — fix at the node
Write the exact profile name the pod requested and load it:
```bash
docker exec -i "$W1" tee /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-audit-write >/dev/null <<'EOF'
#include <tunables/global>
profile k8s-audit-write flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  #include <abstractions/base>
  file,
  deny /etc/secret-data/** w,
}
EOF
docker exec "$W1" apparmor_parser -r -W /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-audit-write

# kubelet retries automatically; the pod then starts
kubectl -n cks-apparmor get pod broken-aa -o wide
kubectl -n cks-apparmor exec broken-aa -- cat /proc/1/attr/current   # k8s-audit-write (enforce)
```

### Why node-side, not pod-side
| Approach | Result |
|---|---|
| **Load the named profile on the node** ✅ | pod's request is satisfied; kubelet starts it; the pod is unchanged |
| Delete + recreate pod without a profile | changes the task's requirement; pod no longer confined as intended |
| Edit pod to point at a different profile | invents a new name; fails the "still references k8s-audit-write" requirement, and `appArmorProfile` is immutable on a running pod anyway |

### The requirement to preserve
- File `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-audit-write` exists on `$W1` with `profile k8s-audit-write` and a `deny /etc/secret-data/** w,` rule.
- The profile is **loaded** (visible in `aa-status`).
- Pod `broken-aa` **still references** `k8s-audit-write` (don't delete/alter it).

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Fix the node, not the pod.** The pod's reference is correct; the node is missing the profile.
- **Name must match exactly** what the pod requested (`k8s-audit-write`), including case. A near-miss name leaves the pod broken.
- **Load on the right node** — the one the pod is pinned to (`$W1`). Loading elsewhere doesn't help a pod pinned via `nodeName`.
- **Don't delete/recreate the pod.** `appArmorProfile` is immutable; the task wants the original pod to come up, and grading checks it still references the profile.
- The kubelet **retries** container creation, so you usually don't need to bounce anything — but if it's wedged you can delete only the container/let the pod's controller retry; here just wait after loading.
- Read the **Events** (`describe pod`) for the authoritative missing-profile message; don't guess the name.
- Remember `-W` so the profile is fully applied before the kubelet's next retry.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n cks-apparmor describe pod broken-aa | grep -i apparmor   # find the missing profile name
docker exec -i "$W1" tee /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-audit-write >/dev/null <<'EOF'
#include <tunables/global>
profile k8s-audit-write flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  #include <abstractions/base>
  file,
  deny /etc/secret-data/** w,
}
EOF
docker exec "$W1" apparmor_parser -r -W /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-audit-write   # kubelet retries -> Running
```
